metadata.title: Capital Added, Withdrawn, or Reduced During the Business
metadata.description: Treat every capital change as a new time segment and total the weighted contribution correctly.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the capital-time model step by step; use timelines and segment ledgers; show intermediate calculations, unit and share checks, and topic-specific remedial feedback. Practice uses fresh values aligned to the approved scope.
metadata.sourceScope: R. S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude, Chapter 14: Partnership (printed pp. 476–492). Approved scope: Partition the business term at every addition, withdrawal, or partial reduction. For each segment, multiply the amount actually invested during that segment by its duration, then add a partner’s segment products. Handle increases stated as a percentage or fraction of original capital, partial withdrawals, complete exits, multiple changes, and equal dates. Avoid counting the same capital twice and verify the segment durations sum to the business term. Use solved examples 3, 5, 13 and objective patterns 21–26, 29, 37–40, 59–64.

content.text: Capital Added, Withdrawn, or Reduced During the Business: Treat every capital change as a new time segment and total the weighted contribution correctly. This lesson builds a partnership model, explains each step, works through examples, and offers fresh practice with targeted recovery.

Capital Added, Withdrawn, or Reduced During the Business asks you to decide what determines each person’s share or assigned amount. Treat every capital change as a new time segment and total the weighted contribution correctly. We will build the model from the agreement, calculate a representative case, and test the result against the original conditions.

Start with the quantity the agreement actually rewards. In ordinary partnership profit sharing, that is the capital made available to the business over time. Each addition or withdrawal changes the capital-time weight from that date onward. Write the partner or user labels and the stated basis before you choose an operation.

The core model is: each partner’s weight = capital × time invested. A capital amount contributes only while it is invested. Each interval therefore contributes capital × that interval’s duration; adding the non-overlapping interval products gives the partner’s full weight.

Split the timeline at every change. Multiply the capital present in each interval by that interval’s length, then add those interval products for that partner. Keep capital, interval duration, and capital-month product in separate columns. Only multiply once the quantities use compatible units; this makes the origin of every ratio term visible.

Worked reasoning: A begins with ₹20,000; after 5 months the capital becomes ₹15,000. Over 12 months the weight is 20,000×5+15,000×7=₹205,000-months. Notice that the ratio comes from relative contribution, not from the order in which partners are named or from who manages the business. Preserve the labels until the final allocation.

When the total profit is known, add the reduced ratio terms to find total parts. Divide the distributable profit by those parts for one part, then multiply by the requested partner’s parts. Do not treat a ratio term itself as a rupee amount.

Use the timeline or agreement to identify intervals before doing arithmetic. Use a ledger with start, end, capital during interval, and capital-months. If a partner’s capital changes, record the new amount only from the date it takes effect; if a time factor is common to everyone, cancel it only after forming the ratio.

A second way to check the model is to rebuild each partner’s contribution independently. Segment durations must be non-overlapping and sum to the partner’s active period. Check the final capital after each change. If the resulting ratio reverses a known relationship—for example, a larger weighted contribution receiving a smaller share—inspect the partner labels and ratio order.

Watch for this error: Do not count the original capital for the full year and then add the change as a second full-year investment. Another frequent slip is to use elapsed time instead of invested time. Mark the start and end of each interval; for a late entrant in a T-month business, invested duration is T minus the delay.

A useful worked check is to allocate the full pool and add the receipts. For partner i, the share is total profit × (i’s weight / all partners’ weights). This fraction must be between 0 and 1 for positive weights, and all partner fractions must sum to 1.

Translate special wording before calculation. A percentage increase may refer to original capital, a withdrawal may be partial, and an allowance may be removed before investment-based sharing. A percentage increase is applied to the stated base, often original capital; write the new amount before building segments. Underline the base of each percentage and state whether the pool is original or remaining profit.

If an unknown amount or date is requested, set up the relationship before solving. Equate the capital-time products in the stated profit ratio, or write a share as its fraction of total profit. Keep unknowns tied to their partner labels and check that a date remains within the business term.

If your first answer seems wrong, revisit the model rather than repeating the arithmetic. Ask: did I use the right basis, include every interval, convert all time units, and use the right total pool? Then substitute the candidate into the original data and recompute the ratio.

For a timed exam, use a compact ledger: partner; event dates; capital in each interval; months; segment product; total weight; share. Reduce large products by common factors only after they are formed, and keep exact fractions until the final currency amount.

Mastery check: explain why the chosen weights represent the agreement, show one intermediate calculation, and verify the final share or sufficiency conclusion. You should now be able to solve the approved scope for capital added, withdrawn, or reduced during the business without relying on a memorized answer pattern.
